Chapter Details: The architecture, governance, functionality and uptake of government digital identity systems and credentials. 30 variables in 5 sections. Contains latest available data. Data collection by Perplexity from a variety of sources.
Definition: Whether individuals can view their data held in the ID database and see how it has been accessed
Comments: No evidence of a portal or mechanism allowing individuals to view their own NINA/digital ID data was found. The APDP law (2013-015) grants citizens the right of access to their personal data, but no dedicated digital ID data-view functionality has been implemented. World Bank Diagnostic (2021) confirms no citizen-facing digital identity services.
revision_notes: World Bank Digital Economy for Mali Country Diagnostic (published 2023, not 2021 as originally dated) confirms no citizen-facing digital identity data-view service exists. DPI Map (updated June 2025) corroborates: no digital authentication, no government portal authentication, and no KYC enablement are recorded for the NINA/biometric ID system, consistent with the absence of a self-service data access portal. Score of 1 (No) confirmed. Year corrected from 2021 to 2023 to match the actual publication date of the World Bank diagnostic.
revised_comments: No mechanism exists for individuals to view their own data held in Mali's national identity database or to see an access log. The Personal Data Protection Act (Law No. 2013-015) grants a general right of access to personal data, but no dedicated digital self-service portal or app has been implemented for the NINA/biometric identity system. The World Bank's Digital Economy for Mali Country Diagnostic (2023) and the DPI Map (2025) both record the absence of citizen-facing digital identity services, including authentication and data-access functions.

Definition: Whether the ID authority and system are subject to general oversight of the courts and judicial review
Value Name: Yes, but not specific to ID
Comments: The Ministry of Justice exercises jurisdictional control over civil registration and handles declaratory judgments (supplementary judgments for adults without birth certificates). General judicial oversight exists but no ID-specific judicial mechanisms were documented. DPI Map records no legally binding redress mechanism for the NINA system.
revision_notes: The 1992 Constitution establishes an independent judiciary (Supreme Court, ordinary courts) with a mandate to safeguard citizens' rights and liberties, but there is no ID-specific judicial or redress mechanism; DPI Map (2025) records 'Legally binding redress mechanism: NA' for the NINA/biometric ID system. The two sources originally cited for this row (a biometric update article on birth-registration reforms and an IRB country report) do not directly address judicial oversight of the ID system; they have been replaced with the Constitution and DPI Map as more directly relevant evidence. Score of 2 (general oversight, no ID-specific mechanism) confirmed.
revised_comments: Mali's identity system is subject only to the general oversight of an independent judiciary rather than any identification-specific court mechanism. The 1992 Constitution establishes the Supreme Court and ordinary courts as guardians of citizens' rights and liberties (Articles 81-82), giving individuals recourse to the ordinary courts for administrative grievances in principle. However, no legally binding, ID-specific redress mechanism exists for the NINA or biometric identity card system, as recorded by the DPI Map.

Definition: Whether procedural rules for collection, storage, and sharing of ID-related personal data are publicly available and established
Comments: World Bank Digital Economy Diagnostic (2021) found no formal data sharing arrangements or protocols for NINA; data sharing is ad hoc and unprotected. No national data governance framework exists. DPI Map records 'Terms of data storage and sharing available: NO' and 'Data handling terms exist: NO'.
revision_notes: DPI Map (updated June 2025) records 'Terms of data storage and sharing available: NO' and 'Data handling terms exist: NO' for Mali's ID system, corroborating the World Bank's 2023 Digital Economy Diagnostic finding of ad hoc, unprotected data sharing and no formal data governance framework. Score of 1 (Not available) confirmed. Year corrected from 2021 to reflect that the World Bank diagnostic was published in 2023, and updated to the more recent DPI Map assessment.
revised_comments: No publicly available procedural rules govern the collection, storage, or sharing of ID-related personal data in Mali. The DPI Map records that terms of data storage and sharing, and data-handling terms more broadly, are not available for the national identity system, and the World Bank's Digital Economy Diagnostic found that data sharing between government bodies is ad hoc and lacks formal protection, with no overarching data governance framework in place.

Definition: Whether national data protection legislation exists and covers personal data linked to the ID system
Comments: Law No. 2013-015 of 21 May 2013 on the Protection of Personal Data is Mali's data protection law. It was amended by Law No. 2017-070 of 18 December 2017 concerning the functioning of the data protection authority (APDP). DPI Map confirms 'National Data Protection Act Exists: YES'.
revision_notes: Confirmed. Law No. 2013-015 of 21 May 2013 on the Protection of Personal Data remains Mali's data protection legislation, amended by Law No. 2017-070 (18 December 2017) regarding the functioning of the data protection authority. Data Protection Africa and the DPI Map (2025) both record the Act as in force. Score of 2 (Yes) confirmed; year retained as 2013 (enactment year) with the 2017 amendment noted.
revised_comments: Mali has enacted comprehensive data protection legislation. Law No. 2013-015 of 21 May 2013 on the Protection of Personal Data establishes the legal basis for collecting and processing personal data and created the data protection authority (APDP); it was subsequently amended by Law No. 2017-070 of 18 December 2017. The DPI Map confirms the existence of a national data protection act covering personal data, including data linked to the identity system.

Definition: Whether a Data Protection Authority or similar body regulates ID data collection and sharing by the ID system
Comments: The Autorité de protection des données à caractère personnel (APDP) was established under Law 2013-015 and launched in 2016. It is independently structured and empowered to investigate, subpoena evidence, and impose sanctions. It has 15 members serving 7-year terms. The DPA is funded directly from the state budget.
revision_notes: Confirmed. The Autorité de protection des données à caractère personnel (APDP), established under Law No. 2013-015, is recorded as active by Data Protection Africa, with powers to investigate, subpoena evidence, and sanction. Score of 2 (Yes) confirmed; year retained as 2016 (launch year), medium confidence as no more recent activity report was located to confirm ongoing enforcement.
revised_comments: A dedicated Data Protection Authority, the Autorité de protection des données à caractère personnel (APDP), oversees personal data collection and sharing in Mali, including data held by the identity system. Established under Law No. 2013-015 and operational since 2016, the APDP is structured as an independent body with 15 members serving seven-year terms, empowered to investigate complaints, request evidence, and impose sanctions, and is funded directly from the state budget.

Definition: Whether the digital ID credential serves as legal proof of an individual's identity as codified in law
Comments: The NINA card was granted national identity card status equivalent to the Carte Nationale d'Identité (CNI) by Decree 2016-0041/P-RM of February 15, 2016. It is accepted as legal proof of identity for police checks, voter registration, passport applications, and other official transactions.
revision_notes: Confirmed and updated. Decree No. 2022-0639/PT-RM (3 November 2022) established the new Carte Nationale d'Identité Biométrique Sécurisée, which by law formally replaces the NINA card, the national identity card, and the consular card as the legally recognised proof of identity, with distribution beginning April 2023. This supersedes the 2016 Decree 2016-0041 basis previously cited, though the legal-proof principle is unchanged. Score of 2 (Yes) confirmed; year updated from 2016 to 2023 to reflect the current legal instrument and card rollout.
revised_comments: Mali's national identity credential carries the force of legal proof of identity. Decree No. 2022-0639/PT-RM of 3 November 2022 establishes the Carte Nationale d'Identité Biométrique Sécurisée, which formally replaces the NINA card, the ordinary national identity card, and the consular card as the certified proof of a citizen's identity, and distribution of the new card began in April 2023. It is accepted for official transactions including elections, passport applications, and police checks.

Definition: Whether formal legislation (act, law, regulation) governs digital identity including identification acts, digital ID laws, or equivalent legislation
Comments: Legal framework for the NINA system includes: Law No. 06-040 (Aug 11, 2006) establishing the NINA number; Law No. 06-024 (June 28, 2006) governing civil status; Decree 2016-0041 (Feb 15, 2016) granting NINA card national ID status; Electronic transactions law 2016-012 (May 6, 2016). A general legal basis exists though DPI Map notes no specific ID or Civil Registry Act.
revision_notes: Confirmed and updated. In addition to Law No. 06-040 (2006, establishing the NINA number) and Law No. 06-024 (2006, civil status), Decree No. 2022-0639/PT-RM (3 November 2022) is the current governing instrument, establishing the Carte Nationale d'Identité Biométrique Sécurisée and mandating enrolment from age 15. DPI Map (2025) notes there is no single, consolidated 'ID or Civil Registry Act', which is consistent with the framework being composed of multiple laws and decrees rather than one omnibus statute. Score of 2 (Yes) confirmed; year updated from 2016 to 2022 to reflect the current governing decree.
revised_comments: Formal legislation governs Mali's digital identity system, though it is spread across several instruments rather than a single consolidated act. Law No. 06-040 (11 August 2006) established the National Identification Number, and Law No. 06-024 (28 June 2006) governs civil status. The current operative framework is Decree No. 2022-0639/PT-RM of 3 November 2022, which establishes the Carte Nationale d'Identité Biométrique Sécurisée, sets its terms of validity, and mandates its issuance. The DPI Map notes the absence of a single consolidated identity or civil registry act, reflecting this multi-instrument legal basis.

Definition: Whether the system and the production of credentials can be managed, maintained and developed by in-country technical staff (as opposed to foreign vendors)
Comments: The NINA/RAVEC system was built and operated under a contract with French company IDEMIA (formerly Oberthur Technologies), which controlled the civil identification database. In 2023 Mali accused IDEMIA of holding the database 'hostage' over unpaid bills. The junta is attempting to migrate to Malian control but foreign vendors (now Chinese Emptech for passport) still dominate. The new AES passport (Oct 2025) is supplied by China's Emptech—foreign vendor dominance continues.
revision_notes: Score revised from 1 (Foreign vendors dominate) to 2 (Partial in-country capacity). Following the 2023 dispute with IDEMIA, Mali's government launched 'Mali Kura Biométrie' in February 2024, a RAVEC/NINA database system built entirely by a 13-person team of Malian engineers ('no foreign providers for maintenance contract'), and national identity card production has since been handled by the Malian company M-SI (with German firm Dermalog providing equipment and training under a technology-transfer arrangement). Passport production, however, remains with a foreign vendor: the contract passed from France's IDEMIA to China's Emptech in October 2025. Given that the core database, its maintenance, and national ID card production are now managed in-country while passport production remains foreign-vendor-dependent, 'partial in-country capacity' better reflects the current position than 'foreign vendors dominate'. Evidence is drawn from multiple corroborating Malian news reports of official government launch events rather than a single primary source.
revised_comments: Management of Mali's core identity database is now handled in-country, while document production retains an element of foreign-vendor dependency. Following a 2023 dispute in which the French vendor IDEMIA was accused of withholding access to the RAVEC/NINA database, the government launched a sovereign replacement system, Mali Kura Biométrie, in February 2024, built and maintained entirely by a team of Malian engineers with no foreign maintenance contractor. Production of the national biometric identity card is carried out by the Malian company M-SI, with the German firm Dermalog supplying certain equipment and training under a technology-transfer arrangement. Biometric passport production, however, is contracted to a foreign vendor, having moved from France's IDEMIA to China's Emptech in October 2025.

Definition: Whether the Ministry of Finance has oversight of the financing and development of the digital ID system
Comments: No evidence of specific Ministry of Finance oversight over the NINA/digital ID system was found. The system is managed under the Ministry of Territorial Administration and Decentralisation (MATD) and the Ministry of Security and Civil Protection. World Bank Diagnostic (2021) notes weak whole-of-government coordination and no specific finance ministry role in ID system governance.
revision_notes: No evidence of Ministry of Finance oversight of the ID system's financing was found. The World Bank's Digital Economy Diagnostic (published 2023, not 2021 as originally dated) records weak whole-of-government coordination and no specific finance-ministry role in ID system governance, which remains with the Ministry of Territorial Administration and Decentralisation and the Ministry of Security and Civil Protection. Score of 1 (No oversight) confirmed. Year corrected from 2021 to 2023 to match the report's actual publication date.
revised_comments: The Ministry of Finance does not have a documented oversight role in financing or developing Mali's identity system. Responsibility for the NINA and biometric identity card system sits with the Ministry of Territorial Administration and Decentralisation and the Ministry of Security and Civil Protection. The World Bank's Digital Economy Diagnostic notes weak whole-of-government coordination on digital identity, with no evidence of a dedicated finance-ministry budget line or oversight role.

Definition: Whether the ongoing management, maintenance and development of the ID system can be funded by sustainable domestic resources
Comments: The NINA/passport system was operated under a Build-Operate-Transfer (BOT) contract primarily financed and run by French company IDEMIA. The 2023 crisis arose because the junta could not pay IDEMIA's bills, causing the system to be shut down. The new AES passport is again supplied by foreign vendor Emptech (China). World Bank Diagnostic (2021) identified a financing gap in the civil registration strategy. Primarily external financing.
revision_notes: Score revised from 1 (Primarily dependent on external funding) to 2 (Mixed domestic/external). The original passport and NINA infrastructure was financed under a French-led Build-Operate-Transfer contract with IDEMIA, which collapsed in 2023 over unpaid bills. Since then, the government has replaced the core database system at no additional budget cost using volunteer Malian engineers (Mali Kura Biométrie, February 2024) and has awarded national identity card production to a domestic company (M-SI). This indicates a shift toward domestic financing and delivery for the core system and card production. However, biometric passport production is now contracted to a foreign vendor (Emptech, China, October 2025), so external dependency has not been eliminated. No comprehensive public financial breakdown of domestic versus external funding shares was found, so this is treated as a mixed model rather than a confirmed shift to primarily domestic funding, and is flagged for human review given the reliance on local news reporting rather than an official financial statement.
revised_comments: Financing for Mali's identity system now combines domestic and external elements, having moved away from near-total dependence on a single foreign vendor. The original NINA and passport infrastructure was delivered under a French-financed Build-Operate-Transfer contract with IDEMIA, which broke down in 2023 amid a payment dispute. The government has since replaced the underlying database management system at no additional budget cost using a team of Malian volunteer engineers, and national identity card production has been awarded to a domestic company. Biometric passport production, however, remains contracted to a foreign vendor, reflecting continued external dependency for that specific credential.

Definition: Whether the system collects biometric data and which modalities are collected (fingerprints, facial image, iris scans)
Comments: The RAVEC census (2009–2011) collected one index fingerprint template encoded into the NINA card's encrypted 2D barcode. The NINA card contains photograph and right-index fingerprint. No iris collection documented. DPI Map (2025) flags 'Uses biometrics: NO' for the current NINA system as the NINA slip (post-2018) lacks biometric authentication capability; however, the underlying RAVEC database was built on fingerprint collection, so fingerprints-only is the accurate historical characterisation.
revision_notes: Confirmed with updated evidence. The 2009-2011 RAVEC census collected a fingerprint and photograph for each citizen, and the successor Carte Nationale d'Identité Biométrique Sécurisée (Decree 2022-0639, rolled out from 2023) and the new e-passport (Emptech, October 2025) continue to be described as biometric, including fingerprints and a photograph, with no evidence of iris capture. The DPI Map (2025) records 'Collects or uses biometric data: NO', which appears to describe the absence of live biometric verification at point-of-service on the current NINA slip rather than the absence of biometric data collection at enrolment; given this is a single conflicting data point against consistent government documentation of fingerprint-and-photo collection at enrolment across three separate credential generations, the fingerprints-only characterisation is retained. Score of 2 (Fingerprints only) confirmed; year updated from 2011 to 2023 to reflect the current card generation.
revised_comments: Mali's identity system collects biometric data in the form of fingerprints and a photograph at enrolment, with no evidence of iris capture. This practice began with the 2009-2011 RAVEC census, which built a biometric database recording a fingerprint and photograph for each citizen, and continues under the Carte Nationale d'Identité Biométrique Sécurisée introduced from 2023 and the new biometric passport introduced in 2025.

Definition: Whether identity records are stored in electronic/digital format versus paper-based records
Comments: The RAVEC census (2009–2011) built a biometric digital database managed by CTDEC. NINA numbers are electronically assigned and a central digital database exists. However, civil registration (RAVEC/CR) records remain largely paper-based and decentralised; the NINA database itself is digital, making this a mixed (partially digital) system overall, but the core ID database is digital.
revision_notes: Confirmed and updated. The RAVEC/NINA database, now managed under the sovereign 'Mali Kura Biométrie' system launched in February 2024, remains a fully electronic biometric database. Underlying civil registration records at the municipal level remain a mix of paper and digital, but the core identity database itself is digital. Score of 3 (Digital) confirmed for the core ID database; year updated from 2011 to 2024 to reflect the current system.
revised_comments: Mali's core identity records are held in a fully electronic, biometric database. Originally built during the 2009-2011 RAVEC census, the database has since been migrated to a sovereign, domestically-built and maintained platform known as Mali Kura Biométrie, launched in February 2024. Underlying municipal civil registration records remain a mix of paper and digital formats, but the national identity database itself is fully digital.

Chapter Details: The architecture, governance, functionality and uptake of government digital identity systems and credentials. 30 variables in 5 sections. Contains latest available data. Data collection by Perplexity from a variety of sources.
Definition: Whether the country has established or is actively developing a national digital identity system, including foundational ID systems that enable authentication across multiple services. Fully deployed means operational nationwide and accepting new registrations.
Comments: Mali's NINA (Numéro d'Identification Nationale) system was established via the biometric RAVEC census (2009–2011) and is fully deployed nationwide. The NINA card received national identity card status by Decree 2016-0041 (Feb 15, 2016). Over 15 million Malians were registered as of October 2016. A new AES biometric passport was launched in October 2025 with Chinese supplier Emptech replacing IDEMIA.
revision_notes: Confirmed and substantially updated. Mali's national digital identity system, originally established via the RAVEC census (2009-2011) and NINA card, has since evolved into the Carte Nationale d'Identité Biométrique Sécurisée (Decree 2022-0639, distribution from April 2023), which by August 2023 had been issued to 5.7 million of 8.46 million eligible citizens on the RAVEC/electoral roll. The underlying database now runs on the sovereign Mali Kura Biométrie platform (February 2024), and a new biometric e-passport was launched in October 2025. The system remains fully deployed nationwide and continues accepting new registrations. Score of 5 (Fully deployed nationwide) confirmed; year updated from 2016 to 2025 to reflect the current system.
revised_comments: Mali operates a fully deployed, nationwide digital identity system. Established through the 2009-2011 RAVEC biometric census and the resulting NINA number and card, the system has since evolved into the Carte Nationale d'Identité Biométrique Sécurisée under Decree No. 2022-0639/PT-RM, with distribution under way since April 2023; by August 2023, over 5.7 million cards had been issued against 8.46 million eligible citizens on the RAVEC/electoral database. The underlying database now runs on a domestically built platform, Mali Kura Biométrie, launched in February 2024, and a new biometric passport was introduced in October 2025. The system continues to accept new registrations nationwide.

Chapter Details: The architecture, governance, functionality and uptake of government digital identity systems and credentials. 30 variables in 5 sections. Contains latest available data. Data collection by Perplexity from a variety of sources.
Definition: Whether the digital ID system is designed to be interoperable across government agencies and with other systems through APIs or data exchange protocols
Comments: World Bank Digital Economy Diagnostic (2021) found NINA lacks interoperability with other government databases; no formal data exchange arrangements or standards; sharing is ad hoc and unprotected. Data is siloed in individual ministries, departments and agencies (MDAs). DPI Map (2025) does not record interoperability as enabled.
revision_notes: Confirmed. The DPI Map (2025) records 'Two or more sectoral use cases enabled: NO' for the NINA/biometric ID system. A September 2025 report confirms that integration between the national identification system and the health ministry's OpenClinic platform is only planned, not yet implemented. This corroborates the World Bank's 2023 finding that the ID system lacks interoperability with other government databases. Score of 1 (No) confirmed. Year updated from 2021 to 2025 to reflect the most recent corroborating evidence.
revised_comments: Mali's national identity system is not yet interoperable with other government databases through APIs or formal data-exchange protocols. The DPI Map records the absence of any sectoral use case enabled by cross-system integration, and a planned link between the identification system and the health ministry's OpenClinic platform, announced in 2025, had not been implemented as of the announcement. Data remains siloed within individual ministries, departments and agencies.

Chapter Details: The architecture, governance, functionality and uptake of government digital identity systems and credentials. 30 variables in 5 sections. Contains latest available data. Data collection by Perplexity from a variety of sources.
Definition: Whether credential is accepted or mandatory for opening bank accounts and accessing financial services
Comments: Under WAEMU/BCEAO AML/CFT rules and Mali's Law No. 2016-020, financial institutions must identify customers using valid ID documents such as the national ID card or NINA card. The NINA card is accepted (not exclusively mandatory as other documents also accepted). KYC compliance requires a valid ID but does not mandate the NINA specifically.
revision_notes: Confirmed. Mali's AML/CFT framework (Law No. 2016-020 and, per a 2025 compliance guide, Law No. 2018-016, together with WAEMU/BCEAO directives) requires financial institutions to verify customers using a valid identification document, such as a national identity card or passport, but does not mandate the biometric identity card specifically over other acceptable ID documents. Score of 2 (Accepted but not mandatory) confirmed.
revised_comments: Mali's national identity credential is accepted, but not exclusively required, for opening bank accounts and accessing financial services. Under Law No. 2016-020 on the prevention of money laundering and terrorist financing, and WAEMU/BCEAO know-your-customer directives, financial institutions must verify customers using a valid identification document, which may be the national identity card, the biometric identity card, or a passport, meaning the specific ID credential is accepted but not mandatory to the exclusion of other documents.

Chapter Details: The architecture, governance, functionality and uptake of government digital identity systems and credentials. 30 variables in 5 sections. Contains latest available data. Data collection by Perplexity from a variety of sources.
Definition: Whether credentials are issued free of charge
Comments: The NINA card is free of charge. ICC-CPI Registry (2018) notes that when NINA card issuance was delayed, the 'Fiche individuelle descriptive' (individual descriptive card) was issued free of charge. The traditional national identity card (CNI) has a low fee of approximately 1,000 CFA francs (under USD 2), but the NINA credential itself is no-cost.
revision_notes: Score revised from 1 (No) to 2 (Yes). The originally recorded score of 1 ('No') is inconsistent with the very evidence cited for the row, which states the NINA card and its 'fiche individuelle descriptive' were issued free of charge. Decree No. 2022-0639/PT-RM confirms that first issuance of the current Carte Nationale d'Identité Biométrique Sécurisée is free of charge, with a fee applying only to renewals. Since the variable asks whether credentials are issued free of charge and the first issuance is free, the correct score is 2 (Yes).
revised_comments: Mali's national biometric identity card is issued free of charge on first issuance. Decree No. 2022-0639/PT-RM, which established the Carte Nationale d'Identité Biométrique Sécurisée, specifies that the first delivery of the card is free, with a fee charged only on renewal. This continues the practice under the preceding NINA card, whose descriptive individual card was also issued at no cost, while the older, separate national identity card (CNI) carried a nominal fee of around 1,000 CFA francs.

Chapter Details: The architecture, governance, functionality and uptake of government digital identity systems and credentials. 30 variables in 5 sections. Contains latest available data. Data collection by Perplexity from a variety of sources.
Definition: Age in years at which an individual becomes eligible to register for digital ID
Comments: The national identity card (CNI) is available to Malian citizens at age 18 (age of majority). The NINA card equivalent status was confirmed by Decree 2016-0041; enrollment is for adults 18+. ICC-CPI Registry (2018) confirms the national identity card is available when citizens turn 18.
revision_notes: Score revised from 1 (>17) to 2 (10-17). Decree No. 2022-0639/PT-RM (3 November 2022), which established the current Carte Nationale d'Identité Biométrique Sécurisée, sets enrolment as mandatory from age 15, superseding the age-18 threshold that applied to the older national identity card (CNI). This places Mali in the 10-17 band rather than the >17 band.
revised_comments: Mali's biometric national identity card becomes mandatory for citizens from age 15. Decree No. 2022-0639/PT-RM of 3 November 2022, which established the Carte Nationale d'Identité Biométrique Sécurisée, sets the enrolment age at 15, replacing the age-18 threshold that previously applied to the standard national identity card (CNI).

Chapter Details: The architecture, governance, functionality and uptake of government digital identity systems and credentials. 30 variables in 5 sections. Contains latest available data. Data collection by Perplexity from a variety of sources.
Definition: Whether registration for digital ID is mandatory, optional, or mandatory for specific groups
Comments: Wikipedia's national identity card policy list records Mali's NINA card as 'Compulsory to all Malian citizens.' The NINA card is required to vote, obtain a passport, and access numerous official services. Law No. 06-044 (electoral law) requires NINA card for voting, effectively making it mandatory.
revision_notes: Confirmed and updated. Decree No. 2022-0639/PT-RM explicitly makes the Carte Nationale d'Identité Biométrique Sécurisée obligatory from age 15, corroborating Wikipedia's characterisation of Mali's identity card as compulsory. Score of 3 (Mandatory for all) confirmed; year updated from 2016 to 2022 to reflect the current governing decree.
revised_comments: Registration for Mali's national biometric identity card is mandatory. Decree No. 2022-0639/PT-RM of 3 November 2022 makes the Carte Nationale d'Identité Biométrique Sécurisée compulsory for citizens from age 15, and the card is required to vote and to obtain a passport, among other official transactions.

Chapter Details: The architecture, governance, functionality and uptake of government digital identity systems and credentials. 30 variables in 5 sections. Contains latest available data. Data collection by Perplexity from a variety of sources.
Definition: Whether non-nationals including refugees, asylum seekers, and permanent residents are eligible to register
Comments: World Bank Diagnostic (2021) notes NINA enrollment includes residents, refugees (via National Refugee Commission), and internally displaced persons/returnees (via National Social Development Directorate). Foreigners also require ID for SIM registration (passport accepted per Reddit/travel sources). Some non-nationals are eligible but not all categories equally.
revision_notes: Confirmed. The World Bank's Digital Economy Diagnostic (published 2023) records that enrolment extends to some non-national categories — refugees, via the National Refugee Commission, and internally displaced persons and returnees, via the National Social Development Directorate — but not a general, unconditional right for all non-nationals to register. Score of 2 (Some) confirmed. Year corrected from 2021 to 2023 to match the report's actual publication date; the Reddit source previously cited has been dropped as it is not an authoritative reference.
revised_comments: Registration in Mali's identity system is open to some, but not all, categories of non-nationals. The World Bank's Digital Economy Diagnostic records that refugees can enrol via the National Refugee Commission, and internally displaced persons and returnees can enrol via the National Social Development Directorate, but there is no documented general provision extending registration to all categories of non-nationals, such as permanent residents or temporary workers.

Chapter Details: The architecture, governance, functionality and uptake of government digital identity systems and credentials. 30 variables in 5 sections. Contains latest available data. Data collection by Perplexity from a variety of sources.
Definition: Percentage of eligible population that has been issued or registered with digital ID credentials
Comments: World Bank ID4D Dataset (2018) estimated 76.8% of total population covered (71% of adults); gender gap with 63% women vs 79% men. Malian authorities in 2016 reported 89% of the population had received NINA cards, with over 15 million registered by October 2016. World Bank ID4D 2018 estimate of 4.25 million unregistered. Coverage is in the 70-89% band.
revision_notes: Score revised from 4 (70-89%) to 3 (50-69%). The World Bank's Global Findex/ID4D regional brief (data from the 2021 Global Findex survey, published 2024) places Mali in the 60-70% band for adult (15+) ID ownership. This is corroborated by official Malian government figures reported in August 2023: 5.73 million biometric identity cards produced against 8.46 million eligible citizens recorded in the RAVEC database, a coverage rate of approximately 68%. Both figures fall within the 50-69% band rather than the previously recorded 70-89% band, which rested on an older 2016 government claim of 89% coverage that pre-dates the current card generation.
revised_comments: Coverage of Mali's national identity system among the eligible population is estimated at approximately 60-69%.
